purpose: Candidate V2 base style delta for object-first/non-human-first card art. This file does NOT duplicate the D4 rendering language - it references global_style_v1.json's existing 'prompt' field as the base rendering style (read-only) and layers V2-specific policy on top. V1 is never modified by this file. A V2-capable compiler (not yet built - see the handoff's 'not yet built' section) would read this file in addition to global_style_v1.json, in place of the V1-only path.
base_style_conflict_disclosure: global_style_v1.json's 'prompt' field (D4's rendering language, reused verbatim by V2 since V2 must not fork or modify it) contains human/character-oriented positive phrasing written for V1's human-led compositions: 'expressive faces', 'bright, appealing eyes', 'elegant stylized anatomy', 'expressive but mature character design', 'clean character silhouettes', and a focal-hierarchy list that names 'supporting people' as tier 3. This is a genuine, disclosed architectural tension, not a hidden one: reusing D4's style text verbatim while also demanding zero humans is self-contradictory unless explicitly resolved. V2's compiler resolves it by inserting base_style_override_clause immediately after the base style block, before any other V2 policy section, so the model sees the character-rendering language paired with an explicit correction rather than left to apply it to a human. A cleaner long-term fix would fork a human-language-free variant of the base style, but that requires explicit authorization to touch/derive from validated D4 production style and is out of scope for this checkpoint. Separately, V1's global_screen_policy field was found to contain a similar but harder-to-neutralize conflict ('Recognition must come from the person, physical tool, device...') and was therefore deliberately excluded from V2's compiled prompt entirely rather than reused-and-overridden - V2 covers screen suppression instead through non_human_protagonist_policy's existing 'no screen images of people' clause plus the dedicated screen_non_human_content containment rule for archetypes (story_culture) where an in-scene screen is semantically present.
base_style_override_clause: The character-rendering, face, eye, and anatomy language above describes the illustration's linework and shading quality only, not a mandate to include a human character. For this card, that rendering quality must be applied entirely to the non-human protagonist, object, animal, or environment described below - no human character, face, or body may be composed into this scene, including as supporting background people.
non_human_protagonist_policy: This artwork must contain ZERO real human presence - no people, no faces, no heads, no hands, no arms, no legs, no feet, no body parts, no human silhouettes, no crowds, no spectators, no players, no workers, no staff, no passersby, no portraits, no photographs of people, no screen images of people, no posters containing people, no reflections containing people, no person-shaped shadows, no cropped humans, and no distant background humans. This rule applies BOTH to the physical scene AND to any media, screen, or display shown inside the scene. Hobby-intrinsic non-real human-LIKE objects are allowed only when unmistakably small physical game pieces with a visible base/stand (tabletop miniatures, chess pieces, figurines) - never a dynamically-posed character with expressive facial detail. Real animals are allowed and encouraged where semantically appropriate (this is a zero-HUMANS rule, not a zero-living-beings rule). STRUCTURAL CONTAINMENT METHOD: do not design a normal human-centered scene and then try to remove the person - design the scene from the start so no human presence is structurally expected, per the matched structural_containment_rules_v2.json rule for this hobby's archetype.
anti_sameness_policy: Do not default to warm golden-hour light, a centered hero object, a cozy warm interior, or floating sparkle particles as the default treatment. Follow this card's assigned composition_diversity_v2.json routes (composition_archetype, palette_lighting_route, effect_level) exactly.

text_policy_v2.principle: The problem is unwanted/generated nonsense text (fake titles, slogans, labels, UI copy), not text as a concept. Do not return to a blanket 'all text is forbidden' rule.
suppress_when: not semantically important to the hobby
likely to render as a fake label, title, slogan, or UI string
allow_when_semantically_natural: abstract calligraphy brushwork (gestural, not a complete readable word, per the existing arts.calligraphy exception)
tiny non-legible print or notation intrinsic to an object
maps as abstract line/shape work, no readable place names
game board markings (abstract symbols, not a readable title)
sheet-music-like notation (abstract staff/note marks, not readable lyrics)
decorative symbols intrinsic to a craft or culture
text_policy_v2.relationship_to_v1: This mirrors V1's already-validated arts_text_suppression_policy and business_text_suppression_policy approach (suppress unwanted generated text, not text as a concept) rather than introducing a new, stricter regime.

brand_safety_policy_reuse_note: V2 reuses global_style_v1.json's global_brand_safety_policy unchanged (generic/unbranded clothing, footwear, equipment, devices, vehicles; no logos/brand marks/swoosh-like or three-stripe-like marks/sneaker-brand silhouettes). No destructive modification of this validated policy is made or planned by V2.
card_ui_suppression_reuse_note: V2 reuses V1's existing full-bleed / no-card-frame / no-rarity-badge / no-title-panel / no-stats-box / no-TCG-shell / no-watermark suppression language unchanged.
not_yet_built: A V2-capable variant of buildPromptV1.js's compileHobbyPrompt() (e.g. compileHobbyPromptV2()) that actually assembles a final prompt string from this file + object_first_rules_v2.json + structural_containment_rules_v2.json + composition_diversity_v2.json + physical_logic_v1.json has NOT been written in this checkpoint. This checkpoint only builds the routing/audit layer (src/objectFirstV2Router.js, src/auditObjectFirstV2.js) that decides WHAT each card should route to; assembling those routing decisions into an actual compiled prompt string is the next engineering step, to be done alongside the recommended small validation batch, not before it.
